"After" as a preposition always expresses the same fundamental idea: one thing follows another. Whatever noun or phrase comes right after "after" is the reference point. What you're describing comes on the far side of that reference point — later, behind, or following it in some way.

Think of a line of people. If you stand after someone, they come first, and you come next.
How to Know When It's Acting as a Preposition

This matters, because "after" can also work as a conjunction or adverb. As a preposition, "after" is always followed by a noun, pronoun, or noun phrase — not a full sentence with its own subject and verb.

  • after dinner — noun ✓
  • after him — pronoun ✓
  • after the long journey — noun phrase ✓

The moment "after" introduces a complete clause (with its own subject + verb — like "after she left"), it becomes a conjunction, not a preposition. You don't need to worry about that here, but knowing the difference protects you from confusion.

1. Later in Time (the most common use)

Something happens at a point in time that comes following another point in time.

  • She called me after dinner. — The call happened at a time that came later than dinner.
  • He arrived after midnight. — He came at some point past midnight.
  • What did you do after the meeting? — What happened in the time that followed the meeting?

An important nuance: "after" only tells you that one thing came later than another. It does not tell you how much later. The gap could be seconds or decades.

  • She sneezed right after stepping outside. — Almost no gap.
  • She recovered after years of illness. — A very long gap.

Both are correct uses of "after."

2. Following in Order or Sequence

"After" can describe position in any kind of sequence — not just time. A list, a ranking, an alphabet, a queue — all qualify.

  • 'D' comes after 'C' in the alphabet. — D is the next one in order.
  • After chapter five, there is a prologue.
  • After you. — A polite phrase meaning: "You go first; I will follow." You are placing yourself behind the other person in the order of movement.

3. Behind Someone or Something That Is Moving

When a person or thing moves, and another person or thing follows the same path behind them, you use "after."

  • The child ran after the balloon. — The child ran in the direction the balloon went, following its path.
  • The dog chased after the car.
  • Close the door after you. — Shut the door behind you as you leave; in the space that follows your passing through.
  • She stared after him as he walked away. — She looked in the direction he had gone.

What unites these examples: one thing is moving, and the other is following its trail or wake.

4. In Pursuit of — Trying to Catch, Get, or Find

This flows naturally from Meaning 3. Here, "after" means someone is actively trying to reach, obtain, or capture something.

  • The police are after the suspect. — They are hunting him; he is their target.
  • She's been after that promotion for months. — She has been trying hard to get it.
  • What are you after? — What is it you want? What are you trying to get?
  • He's only after money. — Money is his sole goal.

This is more about intention and desire than physical movement, but the core idea remains: one thing is following and reaching toward another.

5. Given That Something Happened / Despite Something

This use carries emotional weight. "After" here signals that the situation being described is notable — sometimes surprising, sometimes deserved — in light of what came before it. It asks the listener to hold the earlier event in mind.

  • After all that effort, you deserve a rest. — Given how much effort you put in, a rest is well-earned.
  • After everything she did for him, he never said thank you. — Knowing what she did, his ingratitude is even more striking.
  • How could you lie to me after what I told you? — Knowing what you knew (because I told you), how could you still do that?

The earlier event doesn't disappear — "after" keeps it present and relevant as a backdrop to what follows.

6. In the Style of Someone / In Honour of Someone

This use appears in art, naming, and imitation. "After" means "following the model of" or "as a tribute to."

In art:

  • This portrait is painted after Rembrandt. — It was made in Rembrandt's manner or style; he was the model.
  • A sonata after Beethoven.

In naming:

  • She was named after her grandmother. — She was given her grandmother's name; the grandmother was the model for the name.
  • The university was named after Gandhi. — It carries his name as an honour or tribute.

The link to the core meaning: the new thing (the painting, the name) follows and imitates or honours the original.

7. Asking About Someone's Wellbeing (formal and literary)

This is uncommon in everyday speech but appears in books, formal writing, and older British English. "To ask after someone" means to inquire how they are doing.

  • He asked after your health. — He wanted to know how your health was.
  • She always inquires after the family. — She always asks how the family is doing.

You won't need this often, but you'll recognise it when you see it.

"after all"

This phrase has two slightly different flavours:

"In the end" or "when everything is considered":

  • It wasn't so bad after all. — In the end, it turned out not to be bad.
  • She came to the party after all. — Despite earlier signs that she might not, she came.

"Keep this important fact in mind":

  • After all, we've been friends for twenty years. — This fact matters here; don't overlook it.

"one after another" / "one after the other"

Things happening in a continuous, unbroken sequence.

  • Problems came one after another that year.

"day after day" / "year after year"

Something repeating without stop over a stretch of time.

  • Day after day, she waited for a letter that never came.

Every use of "after" as a preposition — time, sequence, movement, pursuit, naming, or wellbeing — comes from the same root idea:

Something follows something else.

"After" always puts one thing on the far side of another. Master that single idea, and every use of "after" will feel logical, not arbitrary.
